<dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>Decades, not years</dt><dd>On its <span class="lx-term" data-term="diffusion-curve">diffusion curve</span>, electric service went from 8% of U.S. homes in 1907 to over 90% between 1945 and 1950.</dd><dt>Not everywhere at once</dt><dd>Farms passed half about 25 years after town homes; wires had to reach them first.</dd><dt>Gas overtook coal</dt><dd>Piped gas overtook coal as the most common main heating fuel between the 1950 and 1960 censuses. Other fuels changed too; the snapshots do not track homes switching.</dd><dt>What sped it</dt><dd>Networks built, public programmes and a cheaper or better service sped curves up; refining a new source until it could compete took decades.</dd><dt>Say what you measure</dt><dd>A device in homes, a fuel's share of a nation and a share of electricity move at different speeds.</dd></dl>

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Reading a diffusion curve without fooling yourself</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Say the whole.** A share of homes, of families and of electricity are three different wholes; a curve means nothing until its denominator is named.
- **Published points only.** The page reports a year as "between 1945 and 1950" rather than drawing a smooth line through gaps.
- **Starts and ends.** The car survey began when most families already had a car; solar's curve stops at the latest year of data.
- **Services first.** Grubler (2012, abstract) points to energy end use and services, and to the lengthy process of transitions.
